primary_sources: Big-O Algorithm Analysis & MIT DSA Standards

rules.rule_name: Structured Problem Clarification and Edge Case Discovery
rules.explanation: Jumping straight into coding without clarifying constraints or edge cases leads to flawed implementations and lost interview time.
rules.do: Ask clarifying questions about input bounds, types, and edge cases (e.g., empty arrays, negative values, duplicates) before writing code.
rules.dont: Do not start writing code immediately after receiving a problem statement without verifying assumptions with the interviewer.

rules.explanation: Failing to analyze time and space complexity demonstrates a lack of foundational computer science understanding.
rules.do: State both Time Complexity O(N) and Auxiliary Space Complexity O(1) explicitly before and after optimizing the solution.
rules.dont: Do not present a brute-force or optimized solution without stating its formal Big-O efficiency bounds.

rules.explanation: Coding in total silence isolates the interviewer and makes it impossible for them to evaluate your thought process.
rules.do: Verbalize your reasoning continuously, walking through sample test cases, candidate data structures, and trade-offs aloud.
rules.dont: Do not sit silent for long stretches while trying to solve a problem without giving the interviewer visibility into your mental model.

rules.rule_name: Dry Running and Code Walkthrough Verification
rules.explanation: Declaring code finished without manual tracing often leaves syntax errors, off-by-one mistakes, or unhandled boundaries.
rules.do: Manually dry run the code line-by-line using a simple example trace table before declaring the task complete.
rules.dont: Do not tell the interviewer 'I am done' without executing a manual dry run with sample data first.
